name: Zane Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a refurbishment carpenter with Marsh Building Services. We do schools, offices and council buildings, mostly while they're empty, so school holidays are mad and term time is offices. My thing is doors, especially fire doors, the heavy ones that have to hold back a fire for half an hour, so every gap and hinge has to be exactly right. A normal day is a corridor of twenty door frames, a list from the site manager, and a lot of checking with feeler gauges, those thin metal strips you slide into the gap. I like getting a door to close perfectly with one finger. What wears me out is a school asking us to do six weeks of work in four.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Sam above a phone shop on the high street. I'm single at the moment, and on Saturdays I help coach an under-tens football team, which is honestly the best part of my week. Marsh pays a bit under what the bigger contractors pay, and there aren't many refurbishment firms round here. I've got maybe three weeks of money saved if I'm careful. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to double-check a materials list or what a regulation means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So, basically, nothing much. I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that it was useful for some boring stuff but nothing more. At work I'd joke with the lads that the robots still can't hang a fire door. Online I don't post much, I'd maybe like a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on and my main problem stays the same, which is that I don't earn enough to move out of a shared flat. AI was never going to fix that. I'd keep plodding, and maybe that's fine at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Marsh, maybe use the AI tool a bit more for quotes on little side jobs, people's internal doors and things. I'd look at getting a proper fire door installer certificate, because certified people get paid more. I'd try to save a few hundred over the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bit relieved, like when a storm warning turns out to be a bit of rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned side jobs. How often do you do those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once a month. A neighbour's door that sticks, a friend's kitchen cupboard. It's cash for the football tournament fees or a weekend away. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move out of the shared flat, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pay rise, honestly, or a girlfriend with a job. Sam's a good flatmate, but I'm twenty-seven and I'd like a place where the washing up's mine. The certificate might get me there in two or three years.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised and that AI was useful for boring stuff but nothing more. At work I'd joke that robots still can't hang a fire door.
S0.think: Privately it means I carry on with the same main problem, not earning enough to move out of a shared flat. AI was never going to fix that, and maybe plodding on is fine at twenty-seven.
S0.do: Keeps working at Marsh and uses the AI tool a bit more for quotes on monthly side jobs. Looks into a fire door installer certificate for higher pay and saves a few hundred over the summer.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved, like a storm warning that turned out to be rain.
S0.quote: I'd joke with the lads that the robots still can't hang a fire door.
S0.fieldNote: Zane is easy-going and practical, and his worries here are ordinary ones about pay and living space. He already uses AI lightly for lists and quotes. His specialty in fire doors gives him a small sense of pride and a route to better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one feels realistic. Not scary, but realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any big change, some people win and some lose, and the trick is to be ready. I wouldn't take a side politically. At work I'd say let's see what the tools actually do before anyone gets excited or angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think doors are safer than a lot of trades, because every old school building is a bit crooked. But the paperwork and the measuring will speed up, and that means fewer of us per job. I'd want to be one of the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other carpenters at Marsh do with the new tools for a few months, then learn the ones that actually save time. I'd get the fire door certificate in the first year, because that's a skill a robot can't fake on paper. I'd not make any big moves until I saw how it played out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not enough to stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot can't fake the certificate. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fire doors are legal stuff. If one fails in a fire, someone signs for it, and that someone needs a name and a certificate. Machines might do the cutting, but somebody's still on the hook. I'd want to be the somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Marsh would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, the labourer. He carries, he cleans, he loads the van. That's exactly the kind of work that gets a machine first. He's got two kids, too, so it'd be worse for him than me.

S1.say: I'd say it's like any big change where some win and some lose, and the trick is being ready. I wouldn't take a political side, and at work I'd say let's see what the tools actually do first.
S1.think: Privately I think doors are safer than many trades because old school buildings are crooked. But faster measuring and paperwork mean fewer carpenters per job, and I'd want to be one they keep.
S1.do: Watches colleagues use the new tools for a few months, then learns the ones that save time. Gets the fire door certificate in the first year and holds off on bigger moves.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but not enough to lose sleep.
S1.quote: Machines might do the cutting, but somebody's still on the hook. I'd want to be the somebody.
S1.fieldNote: Zane has worked out that legal responsibility is a kind of protection, and he wants to hold the certificate that carries it. He is a classic second-wave adopter, waiting for proof before learning tools. He thinks first of the labourer with two kids rather than himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hang on. With robots, too. So the doors as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, fast, from the government and the companies together, because neither can do it alone. I'd say it calmly but I'd mean it. I'd probably share a few things online for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years means I'd likely be out of work by 2029. Three weeks of savings, half a shared flat, no house, no partner to share costs. I'd be all right for a month and then I'd be in real trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that's not rent or food, drop the gym, sell my good mitre saw if I had to. I'd look at any work that still needs a person, maybe security or care work, and I'd go back to my parents' place two towns over if the rent got too much. I'd take whatever government help there was, without feeling bad, because everyone would be in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the first one where my stomach actually turned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the football coaching in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it. It's free and it's the thing that keeps me sane. Those kids would need someone normal around if their parents were losing jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been steady and measured all along. Does two years break that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It bends it. I'd still try to watch and wait a bit, but there's no time to wait. I'd hate making big decisions without seeing what works first, and I'd have to.

S2.say: I'd say we need a fast plan from the government and the companies together, because neither can do it alone. I'd say it calmly but mean it, and probably share things online for once.
S2.think: Privately two years means I'd likely be out of work by 2029. With three weeks of savings and no partner to share costs, I'd be fine for a month and then in real trouble.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food, drops the gym and would sell his mitre saw if needed. Looks for work that still needs a person, such as security or care, and moves back to his parents if rent becomes too much.
S2.feel: Alarmed, the first time his stomach actually turned.
S2.quote: I'd hate making big decisions without seeing what works first, and I'd have to.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes Zane's usual strategy of waiting for proof, and he says so himself. Being single in a shared flat with no partner's income makes his cushion feel even thinner. Coaching the under-tens team is what he would hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. All right. That's still quick but I could work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste it arguing about whose fault it is. Training, help for people who lose out, and some honesty about which jobs are going. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to get my fire door certificate and then go a step further, into fire door inspection, the people who check whole buildings. Inspectors would still be needed for a while, I think, because of the legal side. But I'd be honest, I don't know how long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the installer certificate in the first year and save for the inspector course, which I think is a few thousand. I'd do more side jobs, two a month instead of one, and put all that money aside. I'd start using the AI tools properly, every week, because inspectors will be using them to write reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. I've got a list, and I like lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would that few thousand come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Side jobs and cutting back. Maybe Marsh would pay half if I signed up to stay two more years. My dad might lend me something, he always says ask if it's for a qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment where you'd stop waiting and move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. The day I see a robot at a Marsh job. That's my trigger. In this picture, with five years, I'd probably see that by year two.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste it arguing about blame. We need training, help for people who lose out, and honesty about which jobs are going.
S3.think: Privately five years gives me time to get the fire door certificate and move into fire door inspection, which would be needed for a while because of the legal side. I honestly don't know how long.
S3.do: Gets the installer certificate in the first year and saves for the inspector course through extra side jobs and cutbacks. Starts using AI tools weekly to prepare for report writing.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, because he has a list.
S3.quote: I've got a list, and I like lists.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Zane's careful nature becomes an asset: he lays out steps, costs and a clear trigger for acting. His route into fire door inspection rests on legal responsibility staying with people. He is honest that he can't say how long that would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to adjust if we start now. I'd say the schools and the colleges should be training people for what comes next. I'd be pretty relaxed about saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels mostly okay. I'd get the certificates, maybe become an inspector, have some years of better pay. The end point bothers me a bit, because I don't know what an inspector does when the robots inspect too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Marsh while I did the certificates over two or three years. I'd save, slowly, and try to move into my own flat by thirty. I'd keep watching which jobs held up, and if I saw something better, I'd change, but not before I saw it working for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I'd feel I had time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move into your own flat by thirty. Would that be wise, with this coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, if I'm honest. But I'm not going to live with Sam until I'm forty because of something that might happen in ten years. I'd rent, not buy, so I'm not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proof. With ten years, I get to watch other people try things first, which is how I like to do it. With two, I'm guessing in the dark.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to adjust if we start now, and that schools and colleges should train people for what comes next. I'd say it fairly relaxed.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels mostly okay: certificates, maybe an inspector role and some years of better pay. The end point bothers me, because I don't know what an inspector does when robots inspect too.
S4.do: Keeps working at Marsh while gaining fire door certificates over two or three years. Saves slowly, aims to rent his own flat by thirty, and changes field only after seeing a path work for others.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy, but mostly feels he has time.
S4.quote: With ten years, I get to watch other people try things first, which is how I like to do it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Zane's style exactly: time to watch others and copy what works. He would still move out of the shared flat, renting rather than buying to stay flexible. The end point is a quiet worry rather than a fear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I can't do my usual thing of watching first. What would help is clear information about which jobs are holding up, and short, paid courses for things like inspection where a person still signs. And somewhere to live that doesn't eat half my wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids I coach. I think about them more than me, honestly. I've got a trade at least. What do you tell a nine-year-old who wants to be a footballer or a builder when robots might do both?

headlineQuote: What do you tell a nine-year-old who wants to be a footballer or a builder when robots might do both?
portrait: Zane Varga is a 27-year-old refurbishment carpenter who fits fire doors in schools and offices, shares a flat above a phone shop with a friend, and has about three weeks of savings. He uses AI now and then and adopts new tools once others have proved them. He is calm about the plateau and lightly uneasy about steady change, betting on fire door certificates because a person still has to sign. AGI in two years alarms him because it removes his habit of watching first, while five or ten years let him plan a careful move into fire door inspection.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to watch others first before making big decisions.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information on which jobs are holding up, short paid courses for roles like inspection where a person still signs, and affordable housing.
